edges.description: Recurrent fever driven by the sustained interferon response rather than by an inflammasome cycle — which is what distinguishes this from the classic periodic fever syndromes.
Acral violaceous lesions, the characteristic cutaneous sign of a type I interferonopathy.
Progressive loss of subcutaneous fat, which in this disease follows the panniculitis rather than occurring independently — the sequence is inflammation first, then loss.
Progressive muscle wasting, part of the same progressive-loss phenotype.
Contractures developing as the inflammatory and atrophic process crosses joints.
Anaemia of chronic inflammation, microcytic here.

nodes.description: The second genetic route into the cascade. Defects in the chaperones that build the proteasome rather than in the proteasome subunits themselves: POMP, which incorporates the catalytic subunits into the assembling particle, and PSMG2, which encodes the PAC2 assembly chaperone. This arm is separated from the proteasome-subunit arm because the lesion is in the assembly machinery and not in the particle it assembles.

nodes.description: Inherited or de novo loss-of-function defects in subunits of the proteasome initiate one of the two genetic routes into the PRAAS cascade. The inducible immunoproteasome catalytic subunits beta-5i (PSMB8), beta-1i (PSMB9) and beta-2i (PSMB10) and the constitutive components beta-7 (PSMB4) and alpha-7 (PSMA3) are the subunits reported in this disease. The reported variants act by reducing subunit expression, blocking propeptide processing, or preventing incorporation into the mature particle.
